quotes.text: Gather unto me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them," the Lord commanded Moses, and "they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone." (Num. 11:16-17.) Thus was the Lord's system of government perfected in ancient Israel. Moses served as the prophet, seer, and revelator; at his side were "the princes of Israel," twelve in number, comparable to the Twelve Apostles, one of whom presided over each of the tribes (Num. 7); then came the Seventy-holy and noble men who also sat in judgment and regulated the affairs of the people. And a millennium and a half later, the Jews still maintained the form of their ancient order; the Great Sanhedrin-either patterned after or descended from the Quorum of Seventy called by Moses-still attempted to rule over the people. Albeit, to their sorrow, those of whom it was composed in time's meridian were no longer the spiritual giants who were qualified to go up into the Holy Mount and see "the God of Israel," as had been their predecessors in office. (Ex. 24:9-11.)

quotes.text: One of the first doctrines to disappear when apostasy conceives in the hearts of mortals is the fact that God is a glorified man. When people repress that doctrine, they forget who they really are and what they may become (cf. the Zoramites, Alma 31:15). One of the first things Joseph Smith learned as the Lord undertook to educate him was that he was created in the literal image of the Father and the Son. Many express outrage at this doctrine, believing that it diminishes God and at the same time presumptuously exalts man. But Joseph Smith did not invent the idea. The Bible plainly speaks of man's creation in the image of God (Gen. 1:26-27); Jacob saw God face to face (Gen. 32:30); God has feet (Ex. 24:10); he has a finger (Ex. 31:18); Moses saw his face (Ex. 33:11) and his back parts (Ex. 33:23) and spoke to God mouth to mouth (Num. 12:8). The "eyes of the Lord" and the "ears of the Lord" occur frequently in the Prophets and in Psalms. In Genesis God walks about in the garden. (Genesis 3:8.)

For centuries thereafter this portable tabernacle, constructed about 1200 B.C. served the people of Israel as their temple and was known as the Tent or Dwelling, The Sanctuary or the Tabernacle. The Tent of Jehovah. It was replaced by a permanent structure built by Solomon about 975 B.C. The Lord specified all the materials, design, clothing, to be used; placement of objects. This is all recorded in Exodus. We can assume that because God is perfect, that all specifications have significance, and that we can profit from a study of them. The path taken symbolically by an Israelite from outside, into the Holy of Holies, was typical or symbolic of man's journey from this world into exaltation. Wood and brass were materials common to the Outer Court, but the glory of Gold was the standard for the precincts of the inner tabernacle. There very placement of the tabernacle in the midst of Israel was symbolically signifi-cant, for the tabernacle symbolized the living presence of Jehovah, thus Israel's life and existence was to center in the Lord. The camp was laid out and organized using God as their central orientation. In actuality, the tabernacle complex consisted of two main divisions; an outer courtyard, and the Tabernacle proper. The courtyard measured 100 cubits, or about 150 feet east to west, and 50 cubits, or about 75 feet north to south. The Tabernacle itself consisted of two chambers or rooms, divided by a veil. The first, which stood 2/3 of the total floor space was called the Holy Place. Only certain officiating priests could enter this place to perform the daily ordinances. The inner chamber, the final 1/3, was called the "Most Holy Place" or the "Holy of Holies." It was a perfect cubit of 10 cubits, height, width and breadth, and could only be entered once a year on the Day of Atonement. Whereas the whole tabernacle complex was viewed as the House of the Lord, the Holy of Holies was seen as the representation of the place where God actually dwelt. Thus the Holy of Holies symbolized the Celestial Kingdom, just as the Celestial rooms in modern temples do. The entrance to the outer court, as well as the Tabernacle itself, faced eastward; It is of course the direction from which light originates in the morning. Oriented toward the light. Inside the courtyard sat the Altar of Sacrifice, made of shittem wood, overlaid with brass. This was the altar on which all the offerings were made. Here the offerer met the Priest, who represented the Lord, in consummating his covenants and was symbolically cleansed. The altar stood 3 cubits high, about 4.5 feet, and was 5 cubits, 7.5 feet square. Four rings were attached at the corners of the altar, through which staves were passed. These staves enabled the altar to be transported. On each corner of the altar a horn was fashioned, as one scholar indicates, these horns were projections on each corner to represent the horns of oxen, and in these the whole force of the altar was concentrated. Horn is commonly used in the scriptures as a representation of power. Horns on an animal are the source of his might and power. One of the root meaning of "horn" in Hebrew is "power." Christ is called the HORN OF SALVATION because of his power to save. Thus the horns of the altar may have signified the power of the Priesthood to administer the ordinances and have the acceptable to Jehovah. Often the blood of the sacrifice on the altar was smeared on the horns, suggesting that power of the atoning blood was being evoked. In this way the children of Israel were reminded of the power of the Lord to save them. The basin was placed between the altar and the doorway of the tabernacle, and was filled with water. It was used for filling the hands and feet of the priests before they officiated at the altar of burnt offerings, and also prior to their entering into the Tabernacle. It represented their need to be clean and presentable before officiating in the sacred ordinances of the tabernacle. The twelve oxen which later supported the laver in the temple of Solomon, represented the twelve tribes of Israel; the water symbolized the baptism required for entry into the House of Israel. Inside the tabernacle were the two rooms. They were separated by a veil. Respectively they symbolize the Terrestrial and the Celestial Kingdoms, while the outer courtyard represented the Telestial Kingdom. The Tent area represented the house or Dwelling place of God. quotes.text: The Ground Plan The Tabernacle is an oblong structure comprising three zones. These are, in descending order of holiness: the Holy of Holies, the Holy Place, and the Court. The structure is oriented longitudinally, on an east-west axis, with the most sacred zone in the west. An outer: perimeter demarcates the sacred area. This is divided into two equal squares. The first two zones lie in one square and the Court constitutes the other square. From the Ark in the Holy of Holies, God reaches out to Israel; from the altar of sacrifice, the Israelites reach out to God. Each seems to be located exactly at the point of intersection of the diagonals of the squares. See diagram, page 155. Ancient Parallels Mobile sanctuaries are known to us from Arab Bedouin practices, pre-Islamic and Islamic, and even from pre-Christian times. They are also documented in Phoenician and Egyptian sources, the latter from the period of Rameses II (ca. 1290-1224 B.C.E.). Furthermore, the method of construction described here in our chapters is now known to be based on well-established Egyptian techniques.' The Celestial Blueprint A prominent characteristic of the narrative in both its parts is the repeated reference to divinely given instructions and celestial patterns for the terrestrial edifice and for its contents.2 Such a conception of a sanctuary is not unknown elsewhere in the ancient world. It is attested as early as about 2200 B.C.E. in the narration of a building project by the Sumerian King Gudea of Lagash. It also occurs in Egyptian texts that treat of similar enterprises. This idea of divine inspiration, initiation, and specification of a religious institution generally communicates the deity's sanction and acceptance of the sacred structure, which is thereby endowed with legitimacy.3 The Tabernacle and Creation The series of instructions for the components of the Tabernacle is made up of seven subsections, each of which is introduced by the formula "The Lord spoke/said to Moses."4 Six of them deal with creativity, and the seventh features the Sabbath law. This latter is explicitly grounded in creation. The association of the Tabernacle with the Sabbath is given prominence in Leviticus 19:30 and 26:2: "You shall keep my Sabbaths and venerate My sanctuary: I am the Lord." Further, the completed Tabernacle is erected on New Year's day, as Exodus 40:17 records. This underscores the idea that a new era in the life of the people has begun and the cosmogonic association of the Tabernacle is thereby strengthened. Finally, other thematic and verbal echoes of the Genesis Creation narrative in our accounts confirm their interdependence.
